title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: from the small print to your own page

questions.prompt: Step 2 of your project asks you to build a page that will make web users want to come to your festival. Tick EVERY item that has to be on that page.

options.text: the dates, and the town the festival is held in
the one thing this festival does that no other does
what it costs to get in, and who pays less
a photograph of a large and cheerful crowd
the names of the other festivals held in the region

questions.explanation: A page that persuades stands on two legs. First the facts a stranger cannot come without: when, where, and what he will pay, with the concessions that may bring his price down. Then the one feature that belongs to this festival and to no other, because that is what makes him choose your page over the next one he opens. A photograph of a happy crowd could have been taken at any festival on earth and proves nothing whatever about yours — go and find the picture of the thing only you do. And listing the region's other festivals is generous of you, but it hands your reader the door out.

questions.prompt: You wrote to the festival office for the price of the group pass and for the dates of the craft market. The reply gives the price and says nothing about the market. Which sentence do you send back?

options.text: You have not answered my second question, and I am still waiting.
Thank you very much indeed for such a quick and helpful answer.
Thank you for the price. Could you also give me the market dates?
I'd like to know more about your festival and the region around it.

questions.explanation: A follow-up does two things in one breath: it acknowledges what arrived, and it names precisely what did not. Thanking the office for the price and asking again for the dates leaves the door open and hands the reader one small, exact task. A reproach closes that door, and does not even remind him what the missing question was. Thanking him for everything pretends the reply was complete, so nothing more will ever come. And widening the request to the whole region asks for far more than you wanted, and buries the one thing you still need.

questions.prompt: Karim's class is attracted by a festival package but has decided nothing yet. He has to tell the office that the offer interests the group, without promising to take it. Which sentence does that?

options.text: We will take twenty of your group passes for April.
We are very interested in your group pass for April.
Please put twenty of your group passes aside for us.
We should like to book twenty places for the April festival.

questions.explanation: Declaring an interest and placing an order are two different acts, and English keeps them well apart. To be interested in something is to say where you stand and no more: the office learns that the class is looking at the offer, it may write back, and nobody has bought anything. Take and book commit the class and buy the passes outright, while putting passes aside has the office hold them in your name, which it may well charge you for. In a message whose only business is to ask questions, that difference is worth real money: say you are interested, ask what you need to know, and decide when the answers come.

questions.prompt: A festival advertisement carries this line at the foot of the page: "*Entry to the craft workshops is not included: a separate ticket must be bought." In the class discussion your teacher asks you to turn the package down with a reason taken from the advertisement itself, and not from your own tastes. Which answer does that?

options.text: I wouldn't take it: I would rather go in September than in April.
I wouldn't take it: package tours are never worth their price.
I wouldn't take it: I have already been to that region.
I wouldn't take it: the craft workshops we came for cost extra.

questions.explanation: Two of these answers describe the speaker and not the offer: a preference for another month and a region already visited are facts about him, and the festival office could argue with neither. Another is a prejudice about package tours in general, which the page in front of him neither supports nor contradicts. The answer that evaluates the advertisement points at a line of the advertisement — the asterisk shuts the craft workshops out of the price, so a group that came for them would be paying twice. All four are opinions, and honest ones; only one of them is an evaluation of what is printed, and only an evaluation can be checked, answered or argued with.

questions.prompt: Read this e-mail: "Dear Sir or Madam, I am interested in your Group Palm Pass. Could you tell me the price for a group of twenty, and the dates of the craft market? I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, Karim Ayari." One of the four moves of a request e-mail is missing from it. Which one?

options.text: It never says where the writer read about the offer.
It never says what the writer would like to know.
It never says that the writer is interested in the offer.
It never closes the message in a polite way.

questions.explanation: The message asks its questions, states its interest and signs off properly — but it starts in mid-air. A festival office runs several offers and advertises them in several places and several months, so until you write that you read about the Group Palm Pass in the March issue of a named magazine, your reader does not know which page you are holding, nor how old the prices on it are. That move costs one line and saves a whole exchange of letters. The interest and the questions are both here, word for word, and the polite close is doing its work at the foot of the message.

questions.prompt: A festival page adds one more line: "Pass holders only may enter our photograph contest." Sonia has a pass and takes photographs. What may she do?

options.text: She may visit the photograph exhibition without paying for it.
She may send in her photographs and try to win the prize.
She may take photographs anywhere inside the festival grounds.
She may join the guided tour reserved for photographers.

questions.explanation: A contest is a competition: you enter it, you send in what it asks for, and you may win something. That is a different promise from an exhibition, which is a set of works of art hung up for the public to look at, and different again from a permission to photograph or from a place on a tour — neither of which this line grants. The word only settles who may enter, and it is the pass in her pocket that lets her in. Read a promise for the kind of thing it is before you read what it gives you.
